claim: The hippocampus has long been implicated in both episodic and spatial memory.
source: The hippocampus has long been implicated in both episodic and spatial memory, however these mnemonic functions have been traditionally investigated in separate research strands.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience supported by extensive prior research.

claim: Episodic and spatial memory functions have been traditionally investigated in separate research strands.
source: The hippocampus has long been implicated in both episodic and spatial memory, however these mnemonic functions have been traditionally investigated in separate research strands.
evidence: This statement reflects the historical approach to studying hippocampal function.

claim: Theoretical accounts and rodent data suggest a common mechanism for spatial and episodic memory in the hippocampus.
source: Theoretical accounts and rodent data suggest a common mechanism for spatial and episodic memory in the hippocampus by providing an abstract and flexible representation of the external world.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to theoretical frameworks and animal research.

claim: The common mechanism for spatial and episodic memory involves providing an abstract and flexible representation of the external world.
source: Theoretical accounts and rodent data suggest a common mechanism for spatial and episodic memory in the hippocampus by providing an abstract and flexible representation of the external world.
evidence: This is based on theoretical models and animal research findings.

claim: Subject-specific neural similarity in the hippocampus scaled with the remembered proximity of events in space and time after learning spatio-temporal trajectories.
source: After learning spatio-temporal trajectories in a large-scale virtual city, subject-specific neural similarity in the hippocampus scaled with the remembered proximity of events in space and time.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The structure of the entire spatio-temporal network was reflected in neural patterns in the hippocampus.
source: Crucially, the structure of the entire spatio-temporal network was reflected in neural patterns.
evidence: This is a key finding from the representational similarity analysis.

claim: There is a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus.
source: Our results provide evidence for a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus and shed new light on its role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing similar neural patterns for spatial and temporal relationships.

claim: The hippocampus plays a role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
source: Our results provide evidence for a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus and shed new light on its role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed neural patterns reflecting the entire spatio-temporal network.

claim: The answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory.
source: It has been suggested that the answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism that is required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory (Eichenbaum, 2014): the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work by Eichenbaum and colleagues.

claim: The common mechanism for spatial navigation and episodic memory is the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space.
source: It has been suggested that the answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism that is required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory (Eichenbaum, 2014): the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on theoretical frameworks cited from Eichenbaum et al., 1999.

claim: Episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life.
source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This definition is attributed to Tulving, 1983.

claim: Episodic memory involves a specific mode of retrieval referred to as recollection.
source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eichenbaum et al., 2007.

claim: Episodic memory involves a specific mode of retrieval referred to as 'mental time travel'.
source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 2002.

claim: Humans must be able to convert relationships between events along physical dimensions of space and time into a mental representation.
source: Notably, this implies that humans must be able to convert relationships between events, for example along the physical dimensions of space and time, into a mental representation so that the arrangement of events is appropriately reflected.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of episodic memory as mental time travel.

claim: Cells in the rodent hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously.
source: In line with this idea, recent discoveries in rodent electrophysiology indicate that cells in the hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously (Kraus et al., 2013, 2015; Mankin et al., 2012) and provide evidence for the notion that memories are, in fact, stored in a multi-dimensional memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999; McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to rodent electrophysiology studies.

claim: Memories are stored in a multi-dimensional memory space.
source: In line with this idea, recent discoveries in rodent electrophysiology indicate that cells in the hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously (Kraus et al., 2013, 2015; Mankin et al., 2012) and provide evidence for the notion that memories are, in fact, stored in a multi-dimensional memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999; McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Memories are dynamically integrated into mnemonic network representations along different dimensions in humans.
source: Findings from fMRI studies in humans also suggest that memories are dynamically integrated into mnemonic network representations along different dimensions (Collin et al., 2015; Horner et al., 2015; Kumaran and Maguire, 2006; Milivojevic et al., 2015; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Schlichting et al., 2015; Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; Zeithamova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: It remains elusive how inter-event relationships along multiple dimensions are combined and converted into a multi-dimensional mnemonic event map.
source: However, it remains elusive how inter-event relationships along multiple dimensions, such as space and time, are combined and converted into a multi-dimensional mnemonic event map, which might potentially support episodic memory.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The hippocampus has traditionally been associated with the representation of space in rodents.
source: In studies with rodents, the hippocampus has traditionally been associated with the representation of space (Burgess et al., 2002; Moser et al., 2008; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), i.e. knowing where events occurred.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in spatial navigation.

claim: Place cells increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed.
source: This spatial code is supported by specific neurons in the hippocampal formation such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), which increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed, and grid cells, which increase firing rate in multiple locations, organized in a hexagonal grid pattern (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: Grid cells increase firing rate in multiple locations organized in a hexagonal grid pattern.
source: This spatial code is supported by specific neurons in the hippocampal formation such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), which increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed, and grid cells, which increase firing rate in multiple locations, organized in a hexagonal grid pattern (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Recent fMRI studies have pointed to similar spatial coding mechanisms in humans as found in rodents.
source: Although much of this research has employed electrophysiology in rodents, recent studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging have pointed to similar mechanisms in humans (Doeller et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2009; Howard et al., 2014; Kyle et al., 2015; Vass and Epstein, 2013; Wolbers et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claim: The hippocampus is crucial for episodic memory in humans.
source: In addition to its role in spatial representation, the hippocampus is also known to be crucial for episodic memory in humans (Eichenbaum, 2014; Norman and O'Reilly, 2003; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Stark and Squire, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on hippocampal function in memory.

claim: Episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner.
source: While it has been acknowledged that episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner (Tulving, 1985), our understanding of the role of the hippocampus for remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time (Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 1985.

claim: Understanding of the hippocampus' role in remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time.
source: While it has been acknowledged that episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner (Tulving, 1985), our understanding of the role of the hippocampus for remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time (Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015.

claim: Situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences have been described in the rodent hippocampus.
source: Recently, descriptions of situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008) and the discovery of time cells in the rodent hippocampus (MacDonald et al., 2011) have sparked a renewed interest in the role of the hippocampus in temporal memory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pastalkova et al., 2008.

claim: Time cells have been discovered in the rodent hippocampus.
source: Recently, descriptions of situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008) and the discovery of time cells in the rodent hippocampus (MacDonald et al., 2011) have sparked a renewed interest in the role of the hippocampus in temporal memory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2011.

claim: Time cells selectively increase their firing pattern at specific time points after a cue had been presented.
source: Time cells have been shown to selectively increase their firing pattern at specific time points after a cue had been presented, while animals were waiting to respond to an odor (MacDonald et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2011.

claim: Time cells exhibited temporally coordinated firing pattern only in specific contexts.
source: Interestingly, the cells exhibited this temporally coordinated firing pattern only in specific contexts.
evidence: This is based on findings from time cell research.

claim: Time cells show remapping behavior similar to place cells when context changes.
source: In a new context, e.g. when delay time was prolonged, some of the previously responding cells ceased to fire or fired at different time points while previously unresponsive cells suddenly began to code for elapsed time, a response pattern akin to spatial remapping of place cells ('retiming').
evidence: This describes the remapping phenomenon observed in time cells.

claim: Time cells represent the specific temporal context of an episode rather than displaying a simple counting function or generic delay signal.
source: Thus, rather than displaying a simple counting function or a generic delay signal, these cells seem to represent the specific temporal context of an episode, consistent with the temporal context model (Howard and Kahana, 2002; Howard et al., 2005).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to the temporal context model.

claim: Time cell findings have led to a re-examination of the hippocampus' role in temporal memory in rodents and humans.
source: These findings have led to a re-examination of the hippocampus' role in temporal memory in rodents and humans (Eichenbaum, 2014; DuBrow and Davachi, 2015; Ranganath and Hsieh, 2016) and to several recent neuroimaging studies in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent review and empirical work.

claim: In predictable sequences, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity.
source: For example, one study found that, in predictable as opposed to random sequences of items, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity (Hsieh et al., 2014), an effect which is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2014.

claim: The pattern similarity effect for sequential items is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
source: For example, one study found that, in predictable as opposed to random sequences of items, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity (Hsieh et al., 2014), an effect which is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2014.

claim: Items are represented differently within event boundaries than across event boundaries.
source: Another study showed that items are represented differently within event boundaries than across event boundaries (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014.

claim: Participants' judgment of temporal distance between item pairs was systematically higher when the pair was separated by an event boundary compared to when it was within an event boundary.
source: Interestingly, participants' judgment of temporal distance between a pair of items was systematically higher when the pair was separated by an event boundary compared to when it was within an event boundary (even though the actual temporal distance was the same for the two types of item pairs).
evidence: This behavioral finding is from the Ezzyat and Davachi study.

claim: Behavioral judgment of across-boundary item pairs as being temporally close was associated with higher pattern similarity during learning.
source: Further, a subsequent behavioral judgment of across-boundary item pairs as being temporally close was associated with higher pattern similarity during the learning task when compared to across-boundary items that were judged to be far.
evidence: This neural finding is from the Ezzyat and Davachi study.

claim: Previous temporal sequence studies investigated temporal sequences independently of the spatial relationship between elements.
source: However, the temporal sequences in these studies were investigated independently of the spatial relationship between the elements.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of prior studies.

claim: Spatial and temporal aspects of autobiographical experiences are coded within the hippocampus across various scales of magnitude, up to one month in time and 30 km in space.
source: Another recent report showed that spatial and temporal aspects of autobiographical experiences are coded within the hippocampus across various scales of magnitude, up to one month in time and 30 km in space (Nielson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nielson et al., 2015.

claim: In the Nielson et al. study, participants wore a camera over four weeks that automatically took pictures throughout the day.
source: Participants wore a camera over the course of four weeks, which automatically took pictures throughout the day.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the Nielson et al. study.

claim: In the Nielson et al. study, participants were scanned with fMRI while reviewing pictures and trying to recall what they depicted.
source: Later, participants were scanned with fMRI while reviewing these pictures and trying to recall what they depicted.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the Nielson et al. study.

claim: The Nielson et al. study had little experimental control over stimulus material with regards to visual properties and degree of familiarity.
source: While providing interesting insight into real-life autobiographical memory, there was little experimental control over the stimulus material with regards to visual properties and the degree of familiarity participants had with the locations.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Nielson et al. study's methodology.

claim: None of the previous studies compared changes in neural pattern similarity from before the acquisition of spatial and temporal structure to after.
source: More importantly, none of the studies mentioned above compared changes in neural pattern similarity from before the acquisition of the spatial and temporal structure to after.
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior research that the current study addresses.

claim: An event map should be abstract to represent aspects of experience that go beyond a direct record of events.
source: Abstract in the sense that it represents aspects of the experience that go beyond a direct record of events, such as being able to extrapolate that taking a specific turn in a city will be a shortcut even before the actual experience has been made.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map based on cited frameworks.

claim: An event map should be flexible to allow for representation of sudden changes in the world.
source: An event map should further be flexible to allow for the representation of sudden changes in the world, such as roadblocks.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map.

claim: An event map should be able to represent relationships along different dimensions concurrently and conjunctively.
source: Thirdly, it should be able to represent relationships along different dimensions concurrently and conjunctively, while still allowing to focus on one dimension depending on task situations, such as for example knowing that the spatial distance between two bus stops is short, but that it could take a long time to get to the destination during rush hour.
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map.

claim: The study used a highly realistic first-person virtual navigation paradigm that led participants through a complex virtual city called 'Donderstown'.
source: We used a highly realistic first-person virtual navigation paradigm that led participants through a complex virtual city ('Donderstown', see http://www.doellerlab.com/donderstown/).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: 16 objects were arranged consistently in a spatial and temporal structure during the learning task.
source: The purpose of this task was to provide a learning experience for participants in which 16 objects were arranged consistently in a spatial and temporal structure, defined through the complex network of inter-object relations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The dimensions of time and space were dissociated through the use of teleporters.
source: We dissociated the dimensions of time and space through the use of teleporters, requiring a high level of flexibility in memory (see Figure 1A for details of the task).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task.
source: To ascertain maximal experimental control, the objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task and all fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during these independent scanning sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: All fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during independent scanning sessions before and after the learning task.
source: To ascertain maximal experimental control, the objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task and all fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during these independent scanning sessions.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach.

claim: Knowledge of the spatio-temporal structure was assessed with a memory test after fMRI acquisition.
source: Knowledge of the spatio-temporal structure acquired during the learning task was assessed with a memory test after fMRI acquisition (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments.
source: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments, including judgments which required higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
evidence: This describes the memory test methodology.

claim: Distance judgments included judgments requiring higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
source: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments, including judgments which required higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the memory test.

claim: Participant-specific spatial and temporal distance ratings were used to investigate changes in neural pattern similarity using representational similarity analysis.
source: The participant-specific spatial and temporal distance ratings from the memory test were then used to investigate changes in neural pattern similarity from before to after the learning task leveraging representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach.

claim: The study investigated whether increases in hippocampal pattern similarity co-varied with the remembered spatial and temporal event structure.
source: More specifically, we investigated whether increases in hippocampal pattern similarity co-varied with the remembered spatial and temporal event structure during the learning task.
evidence: This states the specific hypothesis tested.

claim: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 minutes for the spatio-temporal learning task.
source: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 (mean ± std) minutes for the task (range 52.67–113.06 min), showing high variability in navigation speed.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the learning task.

claim: There was high variability in navigation speed during the learning task.
source: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 (mean ± std) minutes for the task (range 52.67–113.06 min), showing high variability in navigation speed.
evidence: This is observed from the range of completion times.

claim: Navigation times during the last repetition were significantly shorter than during the first repetition.
source: Navigation times during the last repetition were significantly shorter than during the first repetition (21.55 vs 11.60 min, T25 = 6.70, p<0.0001), see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for more details.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data showing learning.

claim: Participants were able to learn the virtual route.
source: In sum, these data indicate that participants were able to learn the virtual route.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the improvement in navigation times.

claim: Participants recalled on average 13.08 ± 3.06 of the 16 items in the free recall test.
source: Participants recalled on average 13.08 ± 3.06 (mean ± std) of the 16 items.
evidence: This is a result from the free recall memory test.

claim: The order of free recall was more influenced by temporal order during the task than by spatial arrangement.
source: The order of free recall was more influenced by the temporal order during the task than by the spatial arrangement, as assessed by correlating the spatial and temporal distances between items during the task with the distance in order during free recall (mean R for spatial distance: −0.01 ± 0.16 [mean ± std]; temporal distance: 0.50 ± 0.40 [mean ± std]; T25 = 4.32, p<0.0003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the free recall analysis.

claim: For temporal judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual temporal distances in 24 of the 26 participants.
source: For temporal judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual temporal distances in 24 of the 26 participants (p<0.05; R = 0.64 ± 0.29 (mean ± std), see Figure 2A for the correlation coefficients across participants and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for participant-specific scatter plots).
evidence: This is a result from the distance judgment task showing good temporal memory.

claim: For spatial judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual spatial distances in 21 of the 26 participants.
source: For spatial judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual spatial distances in 21 of the 26 participants (p<0.05; mean ± std: R = 0.49 ± 0.29); Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the distance judgment task showing good spatial memory.

claim: Correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time.
source: Thus, correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time and slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition (T25 = −2.52, p = 0.019).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the distance judgment results.

claim: Correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition.
source: Thus, correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time and slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition (T25 = −2.52, p = 0.019).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing spatial and temporal memory accuracy.

claim: In 14 of the 26 participants, there was a significant correlation between their spatial and temporal distance judgments.
source: Indeed, we found that in 14 of the 26 participants, there was a significant correlation between their spatial and temporal distance judgments (p<0.05, R = 0.31 ± 0.29 [mean ± std]).
evidence: This is a result showing that spatial and temporal judgments were not independent in some participants.

claim: The two factors of space and time were not independent in most participants' memory judgments.
source: Therefore, the two factors were not independent in most participants' memory judgments and we addressed this in our fMRI analysis (see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation between spatial and temporal judgments.

claim: Both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in spatial distance ratings.
source: Across participants, both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in spatial distance ratings (beta for the factor actual spatial distance: 0.50 ± 0.28 [mean ± std], significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 9.08, p<0.0001; beta for the factor actual temporal distance 0.17 ± 0.19 [mean ± std]; significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 4.48, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claim: The factor actual spatial distance had a significantly greater impact on spatial distance ratings than the factor actual temporal distance.
source: However, the factor actual spatial distance had a significantly greater impact on spatial distance ratings than the factor actual temporal distance (t-test between betas across participants for space > time: T25 = 4.06, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing GLM betas.

claim: Both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in temporal distance ratings.
source: Similarly, both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in temporal distance ratings (beta for the factor actual spatial distance: 0.16 ± 0.22 [mean ± std], significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 3.58, p<0.01; beta for the factor actual temporal distance 0.65 ± 0.27 [mean ± std]; significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 12.16, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a result from GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claim: The factor actual temporal distance had a much bigger impact on temporal distance ratings than the factor actual spatial distance.
source: The factor actual temporal distance had a much bigger impact on temporal distance ratings than the factor actual spatial distance (t-test between betas across participants for time > space T25 = 5.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing GLM betas.

claim: While there was some 'cross-over' between the domain that should be rated and the respective other domain, the domain that should be rated had a greater impact on the judgments both for space and for time.
source: Thus, while there was some 'cross-over' between the domain that should be rated and the respective other domain, the domain that should be rated had a greater impact on the judgments both for space and for time.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claim: Errors in spatial distance ratings were correlated both with actual temporal distance and remembered temporal distances.
source: Indeed, we found that errors in spatial distance ratings were correlated both with actual temporal distance and remembered temporal distances (Fisher z-transformed correlation coefficients tested against zero across participants; actual temporal distance: T25 = −5.39, p<0.0001; remembered temporal distance: T25 = −5.33, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from error analysis.

claim: Errors in temporal distance ratings were correlated with both actual spatial distances and remembered spatial distances.
source: Similarly, errors in temporal distance ratings were correlated with both actual spatial distances and remembered spatial distances (Fisher z-transformed correlation coefficients tested against zero across participants; actual spatial distance: T25 = −4.82, p<0.0001; remembered spatial distance: T25 = −5.04, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from error analysis.

claim: The order in which spatial or temporal distances were probed did not have an impact on biases in the distance judgments.
source: This means that the order in which spatial or temporal distances were probed did not have an impact on biases in the distance judgments.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the test order analysis.

claim: Participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together.
source: Taken together, these behavioral results show that participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together, indicating that they successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral memory test results.

claim: Participants successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
source: Taken together, these behavioral results show that participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together, indicating that they successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
evidence: This is inferred from the accuracy of distance judgments for non-adjacent items.

claim: There is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other.
source: While spatial and temporal distance ratings were correlated with one another in some participants, there is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other, and that the degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-domain bias analysis.

claim: The degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
source: While spatial and temporal distance ratings were correlated with one another in some participants, there is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other, and that the degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the test order analysis.

claim: Participants positioned items with an average distance error of 0.193 ± 0.16 in the map test.
source: On average, participants positioned the items with a distance error (expressed here as the ratio between the displacement error and the side length of the city map) of 0.193 ± 0.16 to the actual item location and performance was variable across participants (range 0.017–0.480, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the map test.

claim: Performance in the map test was variable across participants.
source: On average, participants positioned the items with a distance error (expressed here as the ratio between the displacement error and the side length of the city map) of 0.193 ± 0.16 to the actual item location and performance was variable across participants (range 0.017–0.480, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed from the range of error values.

claim: Pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments.
source: We found that pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments (Z = −3.719, pFDR=0.0005; FDR correction for 15 multiple comparisons, see Methods and materials), as well as their temporal distance judgments (Z = −2.597, pFDR = 0.0078), see Figure 5.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: Pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' temporal distance judgments.
source: We found that pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments (Z = −3.719, pFDR=0.0005; FDR correction for 15 multiple comparisons, see Methods and materials), as well as their temporal distance judgments (Z = −2.597, pFDR = 0.0078), see Figure 5.
evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from the ROI analysis.

claim: Pairs of objects which were recalled as being close together either in space or time had higher pattern similarity increases across all hippocampal grey-matter voxels.
source: More specifically, pairs of objects which were recalled as being close together either in space or time during the task had higher pattern similarity increases across all hippocampal grey-matter voxels.
evidence: This describes the direction of the effect found in the hippocampus.

claim: After removing variance explained by spatial distance judgments, residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with temporal distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus.
source: First, we removed variance explained by spatial distance judgments from the pattern similarity changes in pairs of items in a GLM, and correlated the residuals from this model (i.e. what could not be explained by spatial distance judgments) with temporal distance judgments. We found that these residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with temporal distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus (Z= −1.805, pFDR = 0.041).
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis testing independent contributions.

claim: After removing the influence of temporal distance judgments, residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with spatial distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus.
source: Similarly, when we removed the influence of temporal distance judgments first, the residuals still correlated with spatial distance judgments (Z = −3.719, pFDR = 0.0005).
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis testing independent contributions.

claim: Both the dimensions of space and of time contribute to the observed pattern similarity increases.
source: These results suggest that both the dimensions of space and of time contribute to the observed pattern similarity increases.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analysis results.

claim: The combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments was associated with hippocampal pattern similarity changes.
source: We found that the combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments was indeed associated with hippocampal pattern similarity changes (Z = −3.719, pFDR = 0.0005).
evidence: This is a result from the combined space-time analysis.

claim: The spatial and temporal event structures are not only represented separately, but they are also combined in the hippocampus.
source: Thus, the spatial and temporal event structures are not only represented separately, but they are also combined in the hippocampus, providing evidence that these two dimensions are flexibly integrated to form a spatio-temporal event map.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined space-time analysis.

claim: Pattern similarity across voxels in right hippocampus was significantly correlated with all five factors tested.
source: We found that pattern similarity across voxels in right hippocampus was significantly correlated with all five factors (all pFDR<0.041, significant after FDR correction for 15 multiple comparisons, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from the laterality analysis.

claim: For left hippocampus, only spatial distance judgments and the combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments were significantly correlated to pattern similarity changes.
source: However, for left hippocampus, only spatial distance judgments (with and without effects of temporal distance judgment removed) and the combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments were significantly correlated to pattern similarity changes (all pFDR<0.011), while temporal distance judgments were not (neither with nor without effects of spatial distance judgments removed).
evidence: This is a result from the laterality analysis showing hemispheric differences.

claim: A cluster in right medial to anterior hippocampus showed increased pattern similarity effects for objects that were remembered as being temporally close together.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6, a cluster in right medial to anterior hippocampus showed increased pattern similarity effects for objects that were remembered as being temporally close together in the task (peak MNI:26/−18/−22, T25 = 4.05, pcorr = 0.0178, small volume correction, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a result from the searchlight analysis for temporal distance.

claim: The temporal distance peak in right hippocampus was the global maximum in the acquisition volume.
source: This peak was the global maximum in our acquisition volume and no other effects survived correction for multiple comparisons at a threshold of pcorr <0.05.
evidence: This describes the strength and specificity of the temporal distance effect.

claim: A cluster in right medial to anterior hippocampus showed the highest pattern similarity increases for objects which had the smallest spatial distance in the learning task.
source: Again, a cluster in right medial to anterior hippocampus showed the highest pattern similarity increases for objects, which had the smallest spatial distance in the learning task (see Figure 6, peak MNI:34/−17/−22, T25 = 5.16, pcorr = 0.0046, small volume correction).
evidence: This is a result from the searchlight analysis for spatial distance.

claim: The spatial distance peak in right hippocampus was the global maximum in the acquisition volume.
source: This peak was again the global maximum.
evidence: This describes the strength and specificity of the spatial distance effect.

claim: Partly overlapping regions in right medial to anterior hippocampus represent the spatial and temporal distance between pairs of items.
source: Our results so far show that partly overlapping regions in right medial to anterior hippocampus represent the spatial and temporal distance between pairs of items.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the searchlight analysis results.

claim: For the temporal structure analysis, the effect was still significant after removing the influence of spatial distance.
source: For the temporal structure analysis, the effect was still significant, albeit slightly weaker, after removing the influence of spatial distance (T25 = 3.22, puncorr = 0.0018).
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis in the searchlight approach.

claim: For the spatial structure analysis, the effect was still significant after removing the influence of temporal distance.
source: The same was true for the peak voxel of the spatial structure analysis after removing the influence of temporal distance (T25 = 3.87, puncorr <0.0004).
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis in the searchlight approach.

claim: Part of the overlap in peak regions for space and time may be explained by the two factors being correlated in participants' memory judgments.
source: Thus, part of the overlap in peak regions for space and time may be explained by the two factors being correlated in participants' memory judgments, but there are also significant effects of space and time after statistically removing the influence of the other factor, suggesting that the two dimensions both contribute to pattern similarity increases in right medial to anterior hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analysis results.

claim: There are significant effects of space and time after statistically removing the influence of the other factor, suggesting that the two dimensions both contribute to pattern similarity increases in right medial to anterior hippocampus.
source: Thus, part of the overlap in peak regions for space and time may be explained by the two factors being correlated in participants' memory judgments, but there are also significant effects of space and time after statistically removing the influence of the other factor, suggesting that the two dimensions both contribute to pattern similarity increases in right medial to anterior hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analysis results.

claim: A significant effect was found in right medial to anterior hippocampus for the combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments.
source: We found a significant effect in right medial to anterior hippocampus (see Figure 6B, peak MNI: 32/−17/−22, T25 = 6.07; pcorr < 0.0001, small volume correction).
evidence: This is a result from the combined space-time searchlight analysis.

claim: Pattern similarity in right medial to anterior hippocampus increased strongly when items were close together both in the spatial and temporal domain.
source: This indicates that pattern similarity in this region increased strongly when items were close together both in the spatial and temporal domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined space-time effect.

claim: Objective spatial distances between pairs of items were associated with an increase in pattern similarity across all gray-matter voxels in bilateral hippocampus.
source: We found that objective spatial distances between pairs of items were associated with an increase in pattern similarity across all gray-matter voxels in bilateral hippocampus (Z = −2.85, pFDR = 0.02, corrected for 9 comparisons: 3 ROI × 3 conditions).
evidence: This is a result from the objective distance analysis.

claim: No significant effects were found for objective temporal distance and the combination of spatial and temporal distance.
source: Interestingly, no significant effects were found for objective temporal distance and the combination of spatial and temporal distance.
evidence: This is a result from the objective distance analysis.

claim: Only the factor 'space' was significant in bilateral hippocampus in the 2-way ANOVA of objective distances.
source: We found that only the factor 'space' was significant in bilateral (F1,25 = 8.29, p=0.008) hippocampus and in left hippocampus (F1,25 = 8.84, p=0.006), while neither the factor 'time' nor the interaction were significant in any of the three ROIs.
evidence: This is a result from the ANOVA of objective distances.

claim: There might be a different pattern of results for objective spatial and temporal distances as compared to remembered spatial and temporal distances.
source: These results suggest that there might be a different pattern of results for objective spatial and temporal distances as compared to remembered spatial and temporal distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing objective and remembered distance results.

claim: The remembered distances more accurately reflect the notion of an event map than objective distances.
source: While we think that the remembered distances more accurately reflect the notion of an event map, it would certainly be very interesting to investigate possible differences in the representation of objective distances in future studies, maybe by systematically increasing divergence between objective distances and remembered distances through experimental manipulation.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation and suggestion for future research.

claim: Neural similarity in the hippocampus after learning the spatio-temporal event structure scaled with the proximity of event memories in space and time.
source: We found that neural similarity in the hippocampus after learning the spatio-temporal event structure scaled with the proximity of event memories in space and time, providing evidence for a mnemonic event map in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The findings provide evidence for a mnemonic event map in the hippocampus.
source: We found that neural similarity in the hippocampus after learning the spatio-temporal event structure scaled with the proximity of event memories in space and time, providing evidence for a mnemonic event map in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The hippocampal formation is the key region for coding memory for space and time in rodents.
source: The hippocampal formation is the key region for coding memory for space and time in rodents (MacDonald et al., 2011; Moser et al., 2008; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Pastalkova et al., 2008) and humans (Chadwick et al., 2015; Doeller et al., 2010; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Hsieh et al., 2014; Kyle et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2013; Nielson et al., 2015; Schapiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to rodent and human research.

claim: The hippocampal formation is the key region for coding memory for space and time in humans.
source: The hippocampal formation is the key region for coding memory for space and time in rodents (MacDonald et al., 2011; Moser et al., 2008; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Pastalkova et al., 2008) and humans (Chadwick et al., 2015; Doeller et al., 2010; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Hsieh et al., 2014; Kyle et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2013; Nielson et al., 2015; Schapiro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to human research.

claim: The hippocampus is essential for forming episodic memory, a hallmark of which is vivid recollection, or 'mental time travel'.
source: It is also essential for forming episodic memory, a hallmark of which is vivid recollection, or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 2002.

claim: The two mnemonic functions of the hippocampus have hitherto mostly been investigated in isolation.
source: However, the two mnemonic functions have hitherto mostly been investigated in isolation, even though it has been suggested that the hippocampus supports these different functions via a common underlying mechanism, namely, the representation of multi-dimensional inter-event relationships in memory space (Eichenbaum, 2014; Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior research.

claim: It has been suggested that the hippocampus supports different functions via a common underlying mechanism, namely, the representation of multi-dimensional inter-event relationships in memory space.
source: However, the two mnemonic functions have hitherto mostly been investigated in isolation, even though it has been suggested that the hippocampus supports these different functions via a common underlying mechanism, namely, the representation of multi-dimensional inter-event relationships in memory space (Eichenbaum, 2014; Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The study takes a first step towards demonstrating a common coding mechanism in the human hippocampus by showing that both spatial and temporal relationships between events might be represented by a similar mechanism.
source: Here, we take a first step towards demonstrating such a common coding mechanism in the human hippocampus by showing that both spatial and temporal relationships between events might be represented by a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The study investigates the de novo formation of a spatio-temporal event map by tracking task-induced changes in pattern similarity from a pre-task baseline scan to the post-task scan.
source: Firstly, we investigate the de novo formation of a spatio-temporal event map by tracking the task-induced changes in pattern similarity from a pre-task baseline scan to the post-task scan.
evidence: This describes a key methodological advance of the study.

claim: The pre-post comparison approach enables control for potential effects of stimulus and task confounds.
source: While this approach enables us to control for the potential effects of stimulus and task confounds (see below), most crucially it allows us to investigate representational changes (through comparison of post- vs pre-acquisition effects) as a consequence of encountering a complex event structure during the learning phase.
evidence: This explains the advantage of the methodological approach.

claim: The pre-post comparison approach allows investigation of representational changes as a consequence of encountering a complex event structure during the learning phase.
source: While this approach enables us to control for the potential effects of stimulus and task confounds (see below), most crucially it allows us to investigate representational changes (through comparison of post- vs pre-acquisition effects) as a consequence of encountering a complex event structure during the learning phase.
evidence: This explains the key advantage of the methodological approach.

claim: The study directly relates the specific neural changes observed to the interrelations of the memories that have been formed.
source: Secondly, we directly relate the specific neural changes we observe to the interrelations of the memories that have been formed.
evidence: This describes another key methodological advance.

claim: The participant-specific mnemonic event-map for the newly acquired spatio-temporal structure was mapped out in an extensive post-scanning memory test.
source: We achieve this by mapping out the participant-specific mnemonic event-map for the newly acquired spatio-temporal structure in an extensive post-scanning memory test.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for assessing memory.

claim: The study probed all possible interrelations between the encountered events across spatial and temporal dimensions simultaneously.
source: Here, we probed all possible interrelations between the encountered events across spatial and temporal dimensions simultaneously.
evidence: This describes the comprehensiveness of the memory test.

claim: The full participant-specific temporal and spatial distance maps were reconstructed from pairwise ratings.
source: This allowed us to reconstruct, from these pairwise ratings, the full participant-specific temporal and spatial distance maps which were then used in the representational change analysis of our fMRI data.
evidence: This describes how the memory data were used in the fMRI analysis.

claim: The study combines spatial and temporal aspects in the learning task and uses teleporters to reduce overlap between spatial and temporal distances.
source: Thirdly, we combine spatial and temporal aspects in our learning task and use teleporters to reduce overlap between spatial and temporal distances.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The task is more complex and increases the level of abstraction required to accurately represent the events.
source: This makes the task more complex and increases the level of abstraction required to accurately represent the events.
evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive demands of the task.

claim: All item pairs are defined by a specific spatial as well as a temporal distance.
source: Notably, all item pairs are defined by a specific spatial as well as a temporal distance.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the task design.

claim: For solving the memory task, it is not sufficient to have a notion of two items belonging together or being close, but one needs to retrieve their spatial and temporal position in the task and estimate how close they are in the respective domain separately.
source: Thus, for solving the memory task, it is not sufficient to have a notion of two items belonging together or being close, but one needs to retrieve their spatial and temporal position in the task and estimate how close they are in the respective domain separately.
evidence: This is an inference about the cognitive requirements of the memory task.

claim: Space and time were intertwined to some degree in participants' memory reports.
source: It should be noted that space and time were intertwined to some degree in participants' memory reports.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data.

claim: The generally good fit between responses and actual distances indicates that participants were able to represent the two dimensions separately, at least to a certain degree.
source: However, the generally good fit between responses and actual distances and results from the additional analyses in which we statistically control for the influence of the other factor indicate that participants were able to represent the two dimensions separately, at least to a certain degree.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral results.

claim: The study introduces a novel experimental paradigm that allows investigation of both spatial and temporal aspects of memory and combines a complex episode-like learning task with rigorous experimental control.
source: In this study, we introduce a novel experimental paradigm that allows us to investigate both spatial and temporal aspects of memory and combines a complex episode-like learning task with rigorous experimental control.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution.

claim: Most previous studies in the field have investigated the neural underpinnings of memory either for space or for time.
source: So far, most studies in the field have investigated the neural underpinnings of memory either for space (Bellmund et al., 2016; Doeller et al., 2010; Iglói et al., 2010; Kyle et al., 2015; Vass and Epstein, 2013; Wolbers et al., 2007) or for time (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014; Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In real life, episodes are always embedded in both spatial and temporal context.
source: However, in real life, episodes are always embedded in both spatial and temporal context, as recently demonstrated by a study using GPS and camera timestamps of snapshots of real-life experiences of participants to show that pattern similarity in the hippocampus is sensitive to spatial and temporal distances over large scales of magnitude (Nielson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nielson et al., 2015 and general knowledge.

claim: The study includes both spatial and temporal aspects in the learning task to test how the two dimensions are represented after the de novo formation of an event map.
source: We include both spatial and temporal aspects in our learning task to test, in a laboratory setting, how the two dimensions are represented after the de novo formation of an event map.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The paradigm is well suited to mimic episodic memory formation, due to both the richness of experience and the active nature of the task.
source: This paradigm is well suited to mimic episodic memory formation, due to both the richness of experience and the active nature of the task, in which participants have control and agency over the to-be-encoded events.
evidence: This is a theoretical justification for the experimental approach.

claim: Volitional control is a crucial aspect of the hippocampal role in memory encoding.
source: Volitional control is a crucial aspect of the hippocampal role in memory encoding (Voss et al., 2011) and a sense of self, in turn, may be an essential prerequisite for mental time travel (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A sense of self may be an essential prerequisite for mental time travel.
source: Volitional control is a crucial aspect of the hippocampal role in memory encoding (Voss et al., 2011) and a sense of self, in turn, may be an essential prerequisite for mental time travel (Tulving, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 2002.

claim: In a complex, realistic learning task, analyses might be prone to potential confounds.
source: However, in a complex, realistic learning task, analyses might be prone to potential confounds.
evidence: This identifies a methodological challenge.

claim: Items that are spatially proximal in the task probably also share a similar view, especially in the seconds walking up to the item, and would therefore inflate pattern similarity.
source: For example, items that are spatially proximal in the task (or in real life) probably also share a similar view, especially in the seconds walking up to the item, and would therefore inflate pattern similarity.
evidence: This identifies a potential confound in spatial memory studies.

claim: Items that are temporally proximal would automatically have higher neural pattern similarity due to autocorrelations in the slow BOLD signal.
source: Likewise, items that are temporally proximal would automatically have higher neural pattern similarity due to autocorrelations in the slow BOLD signal.
evidence: This identifies a potential confound in temporal memory studies.

claim: The study limits fMRI analysis to the difference in pattern similarity between two separate blocks scanned before and after the task to counter potential confounds.
source: To counter these potential confounds, we limit our fMRI analysis to the difference in pattern similarity between two separate blocks, which were scanned both before and after the task – an approach taken in several recent fMRI studies (Collin et al., 2015; Milivojevic et al., 2015; Schapiro et al., 2012; Schlichting et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to address confounds, supported by citations.

claim: By focusing on the change in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post, the study can exclude effects of temporal proximity between items in the PVT tasks.
source: One strength of this approach is that by strictly focusing on the change in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post we can exclude effects of temporal proximity between items in the PVT tasks and of a priori differences in neural pattern similarity that some pairs of items might elicit in individual participants, an aspect that cannot easily be excluded by using pairs of autobiographical photographs, for example.
evidence: This explains an advantage of the methodological approach.

claim: By focusing on the change in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post, the study can exclude a priori differences in neural pattern similarity that some pairs of items might elicit in individual participants.
source: One strength of this approach is that by strictly focusing on the change in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post we can exclude effects of temporal proximity between items in the PVT tasks and of a priori differences in neural pattern similarity that some pairs of items might elicit in individual participants, an aspect that cannot easily be excluded by using pairs of autobiographical photographs, for example.
evidence: This explains an advantage of the methodological approach.

claim: Both PVT sessions were identical with respect to stimulus order and timing.
source: Furthermore, both sessions, PVT pre and PVT post, were identical with respect to stimulus order and timing.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Any changes in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post are due to a changed neural representation of objects as a result of the spatio-temporal learning task and the newly formed memories.
source: Any changes in pattern similarity from PVT pre to PVT post (PS') are thus due to a changed neural representation of objects as a result of the spatio-temporal learning task and the newly formed memories.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design.

claim: The combination of advances gives access to study the spatio-temporal organization of memory in humans spanning a triad between an experimentally created objective 'external world', a subjective representation in participants' minds, and how this subjective representation is reflected in the brain.
source: Taken together, the combination of these advances gives us access to study the spatio-temporal organization of memory in humans – spanning a triad between an experimentally created objective 'external world' as simulated with our realistic, life-like task, a subjective representation of this external world in participants' minds as assessed with the extensive memory testing, and the investigation of how this subjective representation is reflected in the brain as expressed in changes in neural patterns associated with an event map.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution.

claim: The existence of place cells and grid cells has suggested that space is represented in an abstract manner, potentially in the form of a 'cognitive map'.
source: For space, the existence of place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005) has suggested that space is represented in an abstract manner, potentially in the form of a 'cognitive map' (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on spatial coding.

claim: The representation of temporal structure has been discussed more in terms of analogous mechanisms like chaining models.
source: In contrast, the representation of temporal structure has been discussed more in terms of analogous mechanisms: chaining models (Axmacher et al., 2010; Jensen and Lisman, 2005) argue that serial events are linked through pairwise binding between succeeding items (through LTP-like mechanisms) and that the recall of one item triggers recall of the subsequent item.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Chaining models argue that serial events are linked through pairwise binding between succeeding items and that recall of one item triggers recall of the subsequent item.
source: In contrast, the representation of temporal structure has been discussed more in terms of analogous mechanisms: chaining models (Axmacher et al., 2010; Jensen and Lisman, 2005) argue that serial events are linked through pairwise binding between succeeding items (through LTP-like mechanisms) and that the recall of one item triggers recall of the subsequent item.
evidence: This describes the chaining model mechanism.

claim: The temporal context model suggests that an episodic element is 'tagged' to slowly changing, random neuronal background activity present at the time of encoding.
source: The temporal context model (Howard and Kahana, 2002; Howard et al., 2005) suggests that an episodic element is 'tagged' to slowly changing, random neuronal background activity present at the time of encoding; this temporal context is then reinstated during recall and provides information about how long ago the episode was experienced by assessing the degree of disparity between the reinstated and the present neuronal background (i.e. the greater the disparity, the more time has passed).
evidence: This describes the temporal context model mechanism.

claim: In both chaining and temporal context models, temporal structure in memory can be seen as a mere by-product of basic neuronal processing.
source: In both of these models, temporal structure in memory can be seen as a mere by-product of basic neuronal processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the theoretical models.

claim: Recent findings about internally generated sequential firing of neuronal ensembles and context-specific time cells are consistent with the notion of a more active mechanism in temporal memory, which might be very similar to mechanisms in spatial memory.
source: However, the recent findings about internally generated sequential firing of neuronal ensembles (Pastalkova et al., 2008) and context-specific time cells (MacDonald et al., 2011, 2013) are consistent with the notion of a more active mechanisms in temporal memory, which might, in fact, be very similar to mechanisms in spatial memory (Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent empirical and theoretical work.

claim: Hippocampal damage leads to impairments in both spatial and temporal memory tasks in humans.
source: In humans, it has also been shown that hippocampal damage leads to impairments in both spatial and temporal memory tasks (Spiers et al., 2001; Konkel et al., 2008) and that the hippocampus is active during active retrieval of temporal sequences as well as spatial layouts (Ekstrom et al., 2011), even though dissociable networks for the two retrieval domains were observed outside of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to patient and neuroimaging studies.

claim: The hippocampus is active during active retrieval of temporal sequences as well as spatial layouts.
source: In humans, it has also been shown that hippocampal damage leads to impairments in both spatial and temporal memory tasks (Spiers et al., 2001; Konkel et al., 2008) and that the hippocampus is active during active retrieval of temporal sequences as well as spatial layouts (Ekstrom et al., 2011), even though dissociable networks for the two retrieval domains were observed outside of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ekstrom et al., 2011.

claim: Dissociable networks for spatial and temporal retrieval domains were observed outside of the hippocampus.
source: In humans, it has also been shown that hippocampal damage leads to impairments in both spatial and temporal memory tasks (Spiers et al., 2001; Konkel et al., 2008) and that the hippocampus is active during active retrieval of temporal sequences as well as spatial layouts (Ekstrom et al., 2011), even though dissociable networks for the two retrieval domains were observed outside of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is from the Ekstrom et al., 2011 study.

claim: One study found an interaction effect in right hippocampus, with increased pattern similarity for spatially far compared to spatially near retrieval trials and the opposite effect for temporally near versus far retrieval trials.
source: In seeming contrast with our results, one study investigating pattern similarity during retrieval of spatially near versus far intervals and temporally near versus far intervals found an interaction effect in right hippocampus, with increased pattern similarity for spatially far compared to spatially near retrieval trials and the opposite effect for temporally near versus far retrieval trials (Kyle et al., 2015) whereas we find a pattern similarity increase both for spatially close and temporally close pairs of items.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kyle et al., 2015.

claim: The discrepancy between the current study and Kyle et al. can probably be explained by methodological differences.
source: However, this discrepancy can probably be explained by methodological differences: we recorded our data not during active retrieval, but during two independent tasks in which participants had to passively view items, and then related the pattern similarity difference between these two tasks to an external behavioral marker, i.e. participants subjective distance ratings, which was collected at a later time point.
evidence: This is an explanation for the difference in findings.

claim: Another study found decreased pattern similarity in hippocampal subfields CA2/CA3/DG between trials in a spatial retrieval condition and a temporal retrieval condition when both domains were correctly retrieved compared to trials when only one domain was correctly retrieved.
source: Another study found decreased pattern similarity in hippocampal subfields CA2/CA3/DG between trials in a spatial retrieval condition and a temporal retrieval condition when both domains were correctly retrieved compared to trials when only one of the domains was correctly retrieved, and the opposite effect in parahippocampal cortex (Copara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Copara et al., 2014.

claim: The data support the notion of a common hippocampal coding mechanism in space and time.
source: Our data support the notion of a common hippocampal coding mechanism in space and time: neural similarity scales with the proximity of event memories in both dimensions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The observed effect is still present for each domain after statistically controlling for the effect of the other domain, suggesting that both space and time contribute to the observed pattern similarity increase, possibly in an additive manner.
source: Notably, while we found that spatial and temporal distance are to some degree correlated in participants' memory, the observed effect is still present for each domain after statistically controlling for the effect of the other domain, suggesting that both space and time contribute to the observed pattern similarity increase, possibly in an additive manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analysis results.

claim: The observed strong effect for the combination of space and time suggests that the two dimensions might be integrated in a common dimension in the hippocampus, i.e. spatio-temporal proximity.
source: The observed strong effect for the combination of space and time further suggests that the two dimensions might be integrated in a common dimension in the hippocampus, i.e. spatio-temporal proximity, supporting the formation of hierarchical structures in a memory space (Collin et al., 2015; Eichenbaum et al., 1999; McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined space-time analysis, supported by citations.

claim: The study provides evidence for a mapping of the entire event structure in the hippocampus.
source: Here we provide evidence for a mapping of the entire event structure in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: The hippocampal event-coding patterns are not restricted to representing event relationships per se, but rather scale with mnemonic distance in a spatio-temporal event map.
source: The hippocampal event-coding patterns are thus not restricted to representing event relationships per se, but rather scale with mnemonic distance in a spatio-temporal event map.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pattern similarity findings.

claim: One alternative explanation for the increased pattern similarity could be that participants covertly retrieve the environment in which they encountered the object and that the effect might be partly related to higher visual similarity in the imagined scene.
source: One alternative explanation for the increased pattern similarity could be that in the second PVT participants covertly retrieve the environment in which they encountered the object in the learning task and that the effect might be partly related to the higher visual similarity in the imagined scene.
evidence: This identifies an alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: Several points argue against the interpretation that effects are due to covert retrieval of visually similar scenes.
source: Several points argue against this interpretation.
evidence: This introduces counterarguments to the alternative explanation.

claim: The views associated with nearby boxes are not necessarily very similar, for example due to rotations during navigation between the boxes or large buildings obstructing the view.
source: Firstly, the views associated with nearby boxes are not necessarily very similar, for example due to rotations during navigation between the boxes or large buildings obstructing the view at one location but not the other.
evidence: This is an argument against the visual similarity explanation.

claim: Increased similarity is observed for temporally close items as well, which due to the teleporters are not necessarily spatially close.
source: Secondly, we observe the increased similarity for temporally close items as well, which due to the teleporters are not necessarily spatially close.
evidence: This is an argument against the visual similarity explanation.

claim: If the effects relied solely on similarity in visual scenes, very prominent pattern similarity increases would be expected in visual areas.
source: Thirdly, if the effects relied solely on similarity in visual scenes, we would expect to see very prominent pattern similarity increases in visual areas.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the alternative explanation.

claim: No cluster survived correction for multiple comparisons outside of hippocampus.
source: However, no cluster survived correction for multiple comparisons outside of hippocampus.
evidence: This is a result from the searchlight analysis.

claim: The findings reflect memory for spatial and temporal relationships, rather than visual similarity.
source: Therefore, we believe that our findings reflect memory for spatial and temporal relationships, rather than visual similarity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the arguments against the alternative explanation.

claim: It is conceivable that other factors in addition to objective spatial and temporal distance impact how a spatio-temporal event map is constructed and remembered.
source: It is very likely that other factors in addition to objective spatial and temporal distance impact how a spatio-temporal event map is constructed and remembered, and it will be very interesting in future studies to identify these factors.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors influencing event map formation.

claim: Event maps are likely not restricted to the physical dimensions of space and time.
source: Such event maps are likely not restricted to the physical dimensions of space and time.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about the generality of event maps.

claim: Elements in memory could be arranged according to a variety of factors, for example social aspects or abstract concepts.
source: Elements in memory could be arranged according to a variety of factors, for example social aspects (Kumaran and Maguire, 2005; Kumaran et al., 2012; Tavares et al., 2015) or abstract concepts (Milivojevic and Doeller, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: It would be interesting to investigate in further studies whether nuanced differences in these dimensions can be read out in hippocampal patterns as well.
source: It would be interesting to investigate in further studies whether nuanced differences in these dimensions can be read out in hippocampal patterns as well.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: If mnemonic relatedness in participants' minds is reflected in pattern similarity, one can reverse the logic and use participant-specific similarity maps to make inferences about their internal record of experience.
source: Another exciting future avenue for research could be that – if mnemonic relatedness in participants' minds is reflected in pattern similarity – one can reverse the logic and use participant-specific similarity maps to make inferences about their internal record of experience (Morris and Frey, 1997; Wood et al., 1999).
