evidence: This is a speculation about future applications, supported by citations.

claim: The present study sheds light on the neural mechanisms supporting the formation of a spatio-temporal event map in memory by leveraging a novel, life-like learning task in combination with rigorous experimental control.
source: In summary, the present study sheds light on the neural mechanisms supporting the formation of a spatio-temporal event map in memory by leveraging a novel, life-like learning task in combination with rigorous experimental control.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The study may be a first step towards mapping out the representation of the external world in the human mind along physical dimensions and potentially also along more abstract ones.
source: More broadly, it may be a first step towards mapping out the representation of the external world in the human mind – here along physical dimensions, but potentially also along more abstract ones.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the work.

claim: A sample size of N = 26 was calculated to be necessary based on an effect size of d = 1.03 from a previous similar study.
source: Based on an effect size of d = 1.03, which was found in a previous similar study from our lab (Milivojevic et al., 2015) in hippocampus, an alpha level of 0.001 (necessary for corrections for multiple comparisons in fMRI data) and power of 0.95, a sample size of N = 26 was calculated to be necessary using G*Power (http://www.gpower.hhu.de/).
evidence: This describes the power analysis for sample size determination.

claim: 26 participants signed up for the study through a University-wide online recruitment system.
source: 26 participants signed up for the study through a University-wide online recruitment system.
evidence: This describes the recruitment procedure.

claim: The mean age of the group was 24.88 ± 2.21 and 11 were female.
source: The mean age of the group was 24.88 ± 2.21 (mean ± std) and 11 were female.
evidence: This describes the demographic characteristics of the sample.

claim: All participants underwent a familiarization phase in Donderstown, so they had good knowledge of the city.
source: All participants underwent a familiarization phase in Donderstown, so they had good knowledge of the city (see below).
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental procedure.

claim: The virtual city environment 'Donderstown' was developed using the Unreal Development Kit for Unreal Engine 3.
source: For the purpose of providing a realistic, life-like episodic learning experience, we developed a 3D virtual city environment using the Unreal Development Kit for Unreal Engine 3 (https://www.unrealengine.com/previous-versions).
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of the virtual environment.

claim: The city consists of a complex network of streets and features residential as well as commercial areas.
source: The city consists of a complex network of streets and features residential as well as commercial areas.
evidence: This describes the structure of the virtual environment.

claim: One side length of the square city roughly translates to 390 m.
source: Relating the eye-level height of the first-person player (assumed to be at 1.60 m) to these arbitrary units, one side length of the square city roughly translates to 390 m.
evidence: This provides a real-world scale estimate for the virtual environment.

claim: Walking one side length of the city takes approximately 36 s, putting the walking speed at 39 km/h.
source: Walking this side length takes approximately 36 s, putting the walking speed with 39 km/h well above normal walking speed.
evidence: This describes the navigation speed in the virtual environment.

claim: The high walking speed was necessary to achieve a sufficient number of repetitions in reasonable time.
source: However, this was necessary to achieve a sufficient number of repetitions in reasonable time.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the high walking speed.

claim: During piloting, it was difficult for most participants to accurately estimate Euclidean distances if the city environment was novel to them.
source: During piloting of this study we observed that it was difficult for most participants to accurately estimate Euclidean distances if the city environment was novel to them.
evidence: This describes an observation from pilot testing.

claim: Some participants showed signs of disorientation, especially with regard to those parts of the route in which they were teleported through the city.
source: Some participants showed signs of disorientation, especially with regard to those parts of the route in which they were teleported through the city (see below).
evidence: This describes an observation from pilot testing.

claim: All participants were required to have taken part in another study from the lab, which pre-exposed them to the virtual city, Donderstown.
source: Thus, all participants were required to have taken part in another study from our lab, which pre-exposed them to the virtual city, Donderstown.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: In the previous study, participants had to learn the names and locations of specific houses in the city and estimate directions between these houses.
source: In this previous study, which took place on a different day (1–21 days prior to participation in the current study), participants had to learn the names and locations of specific houses in this city and estimate directions between these houses.
evidence: This describes the familiarization task.

claim: The familiarization task exposed participants to Donderstown for approximately 2 hr.
source: The task was unrelated to the current task but exposed participants to Donderstown for approximately 2 hr and thereby ensured that they had formed a robust spatial representation of the city.
evidence: This describes the duration of the familiarization.

claim: The familiarization experimental session was crucial to ensure successful learning of the spatio-temporal trajectories.
source: This experimental session was crucial to ensure successful learning of the spatio-temporal trajectories.
evidence: This explains the importance of the familiarization.

claim: Participants did not acquire any knowledge about the position of the wooden boxes or teleporters during familiarization.
source: Notably, participants did not acquire any knowledge about the position of the wooden boxes or teleporters (see Figure 1 and below), as neither was present in the familiarization task.
evidence: This describes what was not included in the familiarization.

claim: Participants were not significantly slower in the 7th round than the 6th round of route learning.
source: Participants were not significantly slower in the 7th round than the 6th round (6th: 13.73 vs 7th: 14.28 min, T25 = −1.04, p=0.3101), suggesting that the participants were already comfortable navigating the route without guidance by that stage.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the route learning task showing successful learning.

claim: Participants were faster in the last round than in the 6th round, indicating better performance despite the lack of guiding cones.
source: Nevertheless, the participants continued to improve and in the last round they were faster than in the 6th, indicating better performance despite the lack of the guiding cones (6th: 13.73 vs 14th: 11.60 min, T25 = 2.82, p=0.0093).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing continued improvement in route learning.

claim: There was no significant correlation between spatial and temporal distances across all possible pairs of objects.
source: There was no significant correlation between spatial and temporal distances across all possible pairs of objects (R = −0.0642, P = 0.4859), suggesting that the two factors space and time did not consistently co-vary with one another.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and confirms the independence of the two factors in the task design.
